extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including how to determine analogous art, level of ordinary skill, differences between claimed invention and prior art, and the prima facie obviousness burden. Covers domain-specific analogy rules (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design) and evidentiary requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 103(c), discovery/substantiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of prior art determined at the time the invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is fixed 'at the time the invention was made' to avoid impermissible hindsight in obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must avoid hindsight and, when necessary, consult MPEP § 2145 for rebutting applicant arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight. The decisionmaker should 'forget what he or she has been taught ... about the claimed invention and cast the mind back to the time the invention was made.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence required to show conditions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant seeking the benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing that subject matter (which qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of §102) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research provisions (for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) invention was made as a result of activities within the agreement's scope; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. Note limits for applications filed before Nov. 29, 1999 and patents granted prior to Dec. 10, 2004; see MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must be analogous prior art to be used in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is proper for use in an obviousness rejection only if it is analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). KSR and Bigio cited: 'any need or problem known in the field of endeavor ... can provide a reason for combining the elements in the manner claimed.' Examiner should determine 'analogous prior art' for obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably pertinent test for analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'reasonably pertinent' a reference must 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deciding reasonable pertinence the examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected (explicitly or implicitly) in the specification; to support reliance on a non-field reference it may be appropriate to include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem. The question often turns on how the problem to be solved is perceived; a narrow/constrained view inconsistent with the specification may improperly limit available prior art. See In re Icon, In re Clay, In re Klein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in structure and function between the claimed invention and prior art carries greater weight than mere classification or class cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification is some evidence of analogy/non-analogy, but courts have found 'similarities and differences in structure and function' to be more important. Examiner should analyze structural/functional overlap (see In re Ellis example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the chemical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical arts, references concerning similar materials, carriers, or chemical problems may be analogous even if in different named arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: references about absorbing biologically active materials on carriers were pertinent across preservative formulations; courts have looked to whether the problem (e.g., electrostatic buildup, dye chemistry) is common across the cited arts, making their teachings pertinent (see Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, In re Mlot-Fijalkowski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the mechanical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In mechanical arts, a broad spectrum of prior art may be relevant where one of ordinary skill would be aware of similar problems across areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple mechanical inventions may warrant inquiry into other areas where similar problems exist; structural similarity (e.g., toothbrushes vs. hair brushes) may make references analogous. See Stevenson, In re Bigio, In re Deminski, Pentec, Ex parte Goodyear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the electrical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In electrical arts, solutions to common technical problems in different high-power or high-frequency contexts may be analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill in the relevant designer art would look to solutions used for the same technical problem (e.g., rate-limiting), then those references are analogous (Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the design arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Design-art analogy focuses on the designer's knowledge of contemporary designs with the same general use; some designs outside the exact article may be analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use as the claimed design. Designers may reasonably know of designs in related furniture or product classes; however, not all designs (e.g., metal ball anode) are analogous to combined insect repellent/air freshener designs. See MPEP § 1504.03, In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention must be considered as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing differences under 35 U.S.C. 103, the question is whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious — not whether individual differences would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both invention and prior art references as a whole. Do not ignore admitted unobvious features of parts of a claimed combination (see Stratoflex, Schenck, In re Hirao); admitted unobvious aspects can render the whole nonobvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to its 'gist' or 'thrust'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to a single 'gist' or advantage disregards the statutory 'as a whole' requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where focusing on a perceived advantage or a single concept led to erroneous obviousness determinations (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit). Examiner must respect express claim limitations and not ignore claim language by distillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source of a problem may be patentable and is part of evaluating the invention as a whole, but discovery alone does not always yield patentability if the solution was obvious from prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery of the source may not render the invention patentable (In re Sponnoble; In re Wiseman example). Examiner should assess whether the discovery materially changes the obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants claiming they discovered the cause of a problem must substantiate that allegation with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate via affidavits/declarations or clear, persuasive assertions in the specification. Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient (In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosed inherent properties are part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties inherent in the claimed subject matter and disclosed in the specification are considered in the 'as a whole' obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the compound/device and its inherent properties disclosed in the specification when delineating the invention as a whole (In re Antonie, In re Papesch). However, obviousness cannot be predicated on properties not known at the time the invention was made even if later shown inherent (In re Rijckaert; see MPEP § 2112 for inherency requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety, including portions that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be considered as a whole, including disclosures that would lead away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art teaches away from the invention (criticizes/discourages the claimed solution), that teaching must be considered (W.L. Gore example). Conversely, mere disclosure of multiple alternatives in prior art does not necessarily teach away (In re Fulton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the hypothetical person of ordinary skill by considering several factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors may include: (A) type of problems encountered in the art; (B) prior art solutions to those problems; (C) rapidity of innovations; (D) sophistication of the technology; and (E) educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC; Custom Accessories; Environmental Designs). Every factor may not be present and one or more may predominate. The person of ordinary skill is not defined solely by credentials and is 'a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton' (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: References not qualifying as prior art may be used to show level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents that postdate the invention or were not widely disseminated (and thus are not prior art) may nonetheless be used to demonstrate the level of ordinary skill and implicit motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such documents can show a motivation to combine implicit in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill (Ex parte Erlich; National Steel Car v. Canadian Pacific Railway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying a particular level of skill not necessary if prior art itself reflects appropriate level
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts regarding level of skill are in the prior art of record, it may not be necessary to specify a particular level; the prior art can reflect the appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held inventions may be declared obvious without a specific finding of particular skill where the prior art reflects the appropriate level (Chore-Time; Okajima v. Bourdeau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the level of ordinary skill is necessary to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention, not to the inventor, a judge, remote-art practitioners, or geniuses (Ryko; Environmental Designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal concept of prima facie obviousness and examiner's initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Prima facie obviousness is a procedural tool allocating who must go forward with evidence. The examiner bears the initial burden of factually supporting any prima facie conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner does not produce a prima facie case, applicant need not submit evidence of nonobviousness. If examiner produces a prima facie case, the burden shifts to the applicant to submit rebuttal evidence (e.g., comparative test data). See In re Rinehart, In re Linter, In re Saunders, and others. Examiner must provide factual support for the prima facie legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a prima facie case requires clear articulation of reasons with rational underpinning
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 must clearly articulate the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; conclusory statements are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require explicit analysis and 'some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning.' The determination depends on the facts of each case (Sanofi-Synthelabo citing Graham). The examiner should make the analysis explicit, though record evidence need not show an explicit teaching of motivation to combine (Ball Aerosol; Federal Circuit guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must step into the shoes of the person of ordinary skill and avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach a proper determination, the examiner must evaluate obviousness from the perspective of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the time just before the invention was made, putting applicant's disclosure aside to avoid hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of the applicant's disclosure must be put aside except as needed to determine differences and conduct the search. Impermissible hindsight must be avoided; the examiner must base the legal conclusion on facts gleaned from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision based on totality of evidence and preponderance standard; reconsider when applicant submits evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate patentability determination is based on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence, and an examiner must reconsider patentability when the applicant submits rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate rebuttal evidence along with the facts supporting the prima facie case, not against the conclusion itself (In re Eli Lilly). Facts established by rebuttal evidence must be considered; In re Oetiker and In re Piasecki discuss roles of examiner's prima facie case and applicant's rebuttal evidence. 'Preponderance of evidence' requires the examiner's evidence to be more convincing than the opposing evidence.
